Issue 12: the ferry vote

Posted on September 18, 2026 by Alice Moreau

This is the twelfth issue, and the first one written in a hurry: the town voted on Thursday night to take over the ferry, and I wanted you to have the numbers before the rumours reach you. The levy goes up by about the price of two return tickets a year, and the new company takes over on the first of January.

The board will be elected at a public meeting next month. If you want to stand, the form is at the harbour office and it asks for nothing more than your name, your address and the names of two people who will say that you are not a pirate. I will write again after the meeting.

The oat cookies from the lifeboat station

Posted on September 11, 2026 by Alice Moreau

Everybody who has ever sat through a lifeboat committee meeting knows these cookies, and nobody knew who made them until the coxswain retired and the tin stopped appearing. It turns out his wife baked them every Sunday for thirty years, and she has kindly let me print the recipe here, with the warning that nobody else has ever got them right.

You need oats, butter, golden syrup, a little flour and more patience than seems reasonable. The trick, she says, is to take them out of the oven while they still look undercooked and to leave them on the tray until they are cold, however loudly anybody complains about the wait.

A week at the boatyard, paid for by the boatyard

Posted on September 4, 2026 by Alice Moreau

The boatyard asked me to spend a week with them and write about it, and paid for the week, so this post is filed under Sponsored, as every such post here is. They did not ask to read it first. What I found was a business of eleven people keeping about two hundred boats afloat, most of them older than anybody working on them.

Half of the work is paperwork now: every hull has its own file, and the files go back to the nineteen fifties. The owner is trying to have them scanned before the damp gets to them, and she would like to hear from anybody who owns photographs of the yard in its early years, whoever took them.
